sec.title: Background
sec.p: Hip fracture is a major cause of morbidity and mortality in ageing populations. Although emerging evidence suggests a role of metabolomic profiles in osteoporosis, their association with hip fracture risk has not been well established. We aimed to investigate plasma metabolomic profiles associated with risk of hip fracture.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We conducted a nested case–control analysis (N = 1234) including 617 hip fracture cases and 617 matched controls (discovery data set) and a prospective cohort analysis including 10,031 participants (replication data set; 475 incident hip fractures) within the Nurses’ Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-Up Study. Conditional logistic regression was applied in the case–control analysis to estimate odds ratios (ORs) per 1 SD increase in metabolite levels, and Cox proportional hazards models were used in the cohort analysis. A total of 653 plasma metabolites were examined, with false discovery rate (FDR) correction applied to control for multiple testing.

sec.title: Findings
sec.p: In the nested–case control analysis, six metabolites related to phospholipid metabolism were consistently associated with hip fracture risk (P < 0.05), with five showing inverse associations. After FDR correction, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, a phosphatidylcholine metabolite, remained significantly associated with lower hip fracture risk (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.87, FDR = 0.02), and this association was replicated in the cohort analysis. At the class level, phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine were associated with reduced hip fracture risk (FDR = 0.01 and 0.05, respectively), with similar patterns in the replication cohort.

sec.title: Interpretation
sec.p: Plasma metabolomic profiles, particularly phospholipid metabolism pathways and phosphatidylcholine, are associated with hip fracture risk. These findings suggest altered phospholipid metabolism may contribute to the development of hip fracture and highlight potential metabolic targets for prevention.

sec.title: Evidence before this study
sec.p: We searched PubMed and Google Scholar from database inception to Dec 1, 2025, for studies in any language using the search terms (“metabolomics” OR “metabolomic profile” OR “plasma metabolites”) AND (“hip fracture” OR “osteoporosis fracture” OR “bone fracture risk”). We also reviewed reference lists of relevant articles. Previous metabolomics studies have reported associations of certain metabolites with bone mineral density and osteoporosis in general. Several cross-sectional and small prospective studies suggested that lipid metabolites, amino acids, or markers of oxidative stress might be related to bone health. However, we identified no large-scale prospective studies that systematically examined the association between a wide range of plasma metabolites and the risk of hip fracture. In particular, the role of phospholipid metabolism in relation to hip fracture risk had not been well established.

sec.title: Added value of this study
sec.p: We used data from two large US cohorts, the Nurses’ Health Study and the Health Professionals Follow-up Study, to investigate plasma metabolomic profiles and risk of hip fracture. In a nested case–control analysis of 617 cases and 617 matched controls, and in a replication cohort analysis of 10,031 participants with 475 incident hip fractures over a median 25.5 years of follow-up, we identified six metabolites involved in phospholipid metabolism that were consistently associated with hip fracture risk, with five showing inverse associations. Notably, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, a phosphatidylcholine metabolite, remained significant after multiple testing correction and was replicated across both study designs. At the class level, both phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine were associated with lower risk of hip fracture.

sec.title: Implications of all the available evidence
sec.p: Our findings extend existing knowledge by highlighting specific plasma metabolomic signatures, particularly phosphatidylcholine and related phospholipid classes, that are associated with a reduced risk of hip fracture. This supports the hypothesis that altered phospholipid metabolism contributes to bone fragility and fracture susceptibility. Together with prior evidence linking phospholipids to osteoporosis and bone mineral density, these results suggest that metabolomic profiling could help identify individuals at an elevated risk of hip fracture and point to phospholipid metabolism as a potential biological pathway and intervention target. Future studies should validate these associations in other populations and explore the mechanistic role of phospholipid metabolism in bone health and fracture prevention.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Hip fractures are among the most severe complications of osteoporosis and are a major cause of morbidity, long-term disability, and mortality in older adults.1, 2, 3 According to the Global Burden of Disease (2019), the prevalence of hip fractures in adults aged 55 years and older was 1191 per 100,000 people, contributing to 131 years lived with disability per 100,000 population.4 Despite advances in osteoporosis prevention and treatment strategies,5, 6, 7, 8 hip fractures continue to pose significant clinical and economic challenges, with their annual incidence is expected to double by 2050 as the population ages.1

Given the metabolic underpinnings of osteoporosis, metabolomic profiling offers a promising avenue for identifying biomarkers associated with bone health. However, single biomarkers, such as beta-C-terminal telopeptide, have shown limited ability to improve fracture prediction.9 In contrast, circulating metabolites may provide a more comprehensive assessment of bone metabolism and health, reflecting the cumulative effects of genetic and environmental influences.10

Previous studies have explored associations between plasma metabolites and bone mineral density (BMD) or osteoporosis, but most have been cross-sectional in design.9,11, 12, 13, 14 A systematic review highlighted the potential of metabolomics for clinical applications in osteoporosis; however, findings on metabolite associations with BMD remain inconsistent.15 Moreover, prospective studies investigating metabolomic profiles in relation to hip fracture risk—one of the most severe consequences of osteoporosis—are limited. While a recent study identified metabolites associated with BMD and overall osteoporotic fracture risk,16 it did not specifically examine their associations with hip fractures. Additionally, the sample sizes of existing studies are often small, limiting their generalisability. Prospective studies are needed to identify metabolites that are associated with the future risk of developing hip fracture.

To address this gap, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of plasma metabolomic profiles and hip fracture risk in a nested case–control analysis, followed by replication in a prospective cohort study within two well-established U.S. cohorts of females and males. We aimed to explore associations of individual metabolites and metabolomic classes with subsequent risk of hip fracture.

sec.title: Data source: nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and Health Professionals Follow-Up study (HPFS)
sec.p: This study was conducted within the Nurses’ Health Study (NHS) and Health Professionals Follow-up Study (HPFS), two large prospective cohorts with ongoing biennial follow-up. The NHS was initiated in 1976 with 121,700 female registered nurses aged 30–55 years,17 and HPFS began in 1986 with 51,529 male health professionals aged 40–75 years.18 Participants have provided lifestyle and medical data through self-reported questionnaires with a follow-up rate exceeding 90% of the eligible person-time.

sec.title: Ethics
sec.p: The study protocol for each cohort and this hip fracture metabolomics project was approved by the institutional review boards (IRBs) of Brigham and Women's Hospital and Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health (IRB24-0407; 1999P011114). At enrolment, participants received a letter being informed about the intent of the research and the IRBs allowed participants' completion of the self-administered questionnaire to be considered as implied consent. This research adheres to the 2024 Declaration of Helsinki ethical principles.

sec.title: Blood collection
sec.p: Blood samples were collected between 1989 and 1990 from 32,826 NHS participants, with a subset of 18,743 providing a second sample between 2000 and 2001. In HPFS, blood samples were collected between 1993 and 1995 from 18,159 participants. Participants arranged for blood draws and shipped their samples via overnight courier, with 95% of samples arriving within 24 h.19 Plasma aliquots were stored in liquid nitrogen freezers at ≤−130 °C. For NHS participants, blood samples from the second collection were used. Hip fractures occurring after blood collection were identified through June 1, 2016, in NHS and January 1, 2016, in HPFS.

A nested case–control study (N = 1234) was conducted, including 617 incident hip fracture cases (321 from NHS and 296 from HPFS), with blood samples collected prior to diagnosis. Each hip fracture case was individually matched to one control remained free of hip fracture by the end of follow-up (cumulative sampling) and controls were selected without replacement. Cases were matched 1:1 with controls based on age at blood collection (within 25 months, 90% matched within 12 months), cohort/sex, month and year of blood collection, time of day of blood draw (morning vs. other), fasting status, and ancestry (although both cohorts are >90% non-Hispanic White). For females, menopausal status and hormone therapy use at blood draw were also considered as matching factors. Matching factors and covariates were determined from questionnaire data at blood collection or the most recent biennial questionnaire preceding it.

A replication cohort analysis included 10,031 participants (7577 from NHS and 2454 from HPFS) from 14 prior metabolomics sub-studies for other health outcomes (Table S1).20 To avoid hip fracture case overlap, individuals with prior hip fractures at blood draw or those included in the nested case–control study were excluded from the replication analysis. The workflow for participant inclusion in the nested case–control and replication cohort studies is shown in Figure S1.

sec.title: Ascertainment of hip fracture
sec.p: Hip fractures were identified through self-reported biennial questionnaires, with validation studies demonstrating high reliability that all reported hip fractures in a random subsample of the cohort were confirmed upon review of medical records.21 Supplemental questionnaires confirmed fracture details, including bone site, date, and trauma circumstances. High-trauma fractures (e.g., motor vehicle accidents, horseback riding, skiing) were excluded to focus on osteoporotic fractures. Only fractures of the proximal femur were classified as hip fractures.

sec.title: Metabolomics assays
sec.p: Metabolomic profiling for the nested case–control study was conducted at Metabolon (Morrisville, NC, USA) using ultra-performance liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC/MS).22 All paired case and control samples were handled identically with the case–control status blinded to the assay lab and were processed in the same analytical run in random order. Briefly, after sample accession and preparation, each sample was divided into one backup aliquot and four aliquots for the different measurement methods: 1) acidic positive ion conditions optimised for more hydrophilic compounds, 2) acidic positive ion conditions optimised for more hydrophobic compounds, 3) basic negative ion optimised conditions using a separate dedicated C18 column, and 4) negative ionisation following elution from a hydrophilic interaction liquid chromatography (HILIC) column. A total of 653 unique known metabolites (518 metabolites measured in NHS, and 360 metabolites measured in HPFS) were analysed after excluding those affected by delayed blood processing or with >70% missing data (Figure S2). In the cohort analysis, plasma metabolites were measured using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC/MS) at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard.23 After similar exclusion criteria, 45 overlapped metabolites, including 29 metabolites from the phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine classes, were included for replication. Our previous study showed that, on average, the intrapersonal stability of plasma metabolomic measurements over 10 years is similar to that of cholesterol, the most commonly used risk biomarker for cardiovascular disease.24

sec.title: Covariates
sec.p: Covariates included demographic and anthropometric data such as date of birth, height, weight, and self-reported sex and ancestry. Weight was assessed biennially, with validation studies demonstrating a high correlation (r = 0.97) with directly measured values.25 BMI (kg/m2) was calculated from self-reported height and weight. Lifestyle factors, including smoking, postmenopausal hormone therapy, diuretic (thiazide or loop) use, and bisphosphonate use, were assessed biennially. Medical histories of hypertension, diabetes, and osteoporosis were previously validated within the NHS and HPFS cohorts.21,26,27 Dietary intake, including dietary and supplemental calcium, vitamin D, caffeine, protein, and alcohol consumption, was assessed via semi-quantitative food frequency questionnaires, which have been extensively validated.28 Physical activity, expressed as metabolic equivalent task (MET) hours per week, was self-reported and previously validated (r = 0.79).29

Plasma biomarkers of bone metabolism, including beta-C-terminal telopeptide, parathyroid hormone, osteocalcin, sclerostin, and 25(OH)-vitamin D, were also measured at the same time as the metabolomic profiling. We measured total osteocalcin and beta-C-terminal telopeptide using electrochemiluminescence immunoassays (Roche E Modular system; for osteocalcin, the lowest detection limit of this assay is 0.50 ng/mL and the day-to-day imprecision values at concentrations of 7.04, 25.5 and 78.1 ng/mL are 1.6, 1.4 and 1.5%, respectively; for beta-C-terminal telopeptide, the lowest detection limit of this assay is 0.01 ng/mL and the day-to-day imprecision values at concentrations of 0.08, 0.39 and 3.59 ng/mL are 4.7, 4.3 and 1.6%, respectively). We measured sclerostin using a quantitative sandwich enzyme immunoassay (Alpco Diagnostics, Salem, NH; sensitivity of 8.9 pmol/L and a run-to-run imprecision at sclerostin concentrations of 13 and 35 pmol/L of 5.0 and 6.0%, respectively).

sec.title: Statistics
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using log-transformed and standardised metabolite data (z-scores) to enhance interpretability and comparability across metabolites. In the nested case–control analysis using cumulative sampling strategy, odds ratios (ORs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for incident hip fracture were estimated per one standard deviation increase in metabolite levels using multivariable-adjusted conditional logistic regression. To test for linearity, we modelled the association between plasma metabolites and hip fracture risk using restricted cubic splines and a Wald test P < 0.05 for the restricted cubic spline terms were considered a departure from linearity. Conditional logistic regression models accounted for the matching factors, and additional covariates including, age, BMI, osteoporosis history, alcohol intake, plasma vitamin D, and sclerostin levels were adjusted for in the models. These covariates were selected based on their biological relevance and observed differential distribution between cases and controls (Figure S3). Multiple comparisons were addressed using the false discovery rate (FDR), with FDR < 0.05 considered statistically significant and FDR < 0.2 considered nominally significant.10 Metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA) was used to evaluate associations between metabolite classes and hip fracture risk.30 We calculated the normalised enrichment scores (NES), which typically range from −3 to +3, along with the FDR values in the MSEA analysis. A positive NES indicates enrichment of metabolites, whereas a negative NES reflects depletion; the magnitude of the score reflects the strength of enrichment, with values farther from zero indicating stronger associations. Spearman correlation analysis was performed to assess the associations between candidate metabolites and plasma biomarkers related to hip fracture.

For the cohort analysis, time-to-event was calculated from blood draw to hip fracture diagnosis, death, date of the last return of a valid follow-up questionnaire, or end of follow-up (June 2016 for NHS and January 2016 for HPFS), whichever occurred first. Cox proportional hazards regression models using follow-up duration (months) as timescale estimated hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% CIs of candidate metabolites for hip fracture incidence, adjusting for fasting status, season of blood collection, sub-study outcome (Table S1), case–control status in the 14 prior sub-studies, age, BMI, osteoporosis history, alcohol intake, and postmenopausal status/hormone therapy use (NHS only). We verified the proportional hazards assumption using Schoenfeld residuals and assessed linearity for continuous variables with restricted cubic splines; no violations of these assumptions were observed. We conducted an additional analysis treating death as a competing event using a Fine–Grey hazard model that expressed associations as subdistribution hazard ratios.31

The rates for missing covariates were low in the analyses. Any missing values for physical activity, alcohol intake, nutrients intake, BMI were first replaced by valid values in the previous questionnaire cycle given the biennial survey design of the NHS and HPFS cohorts. For the remaining missing data and plasma biomarkers, we replaced the missing values with the median values in the cohort (Table S2).

Given the discovery-replication design, results from the discovery dataset were tested in the replication dataset and thus, multiple comparison corrections were not applied to the replication analysis in the cohort study. All statistical tests were two-sided, and analyses were performed using SAS 9.4 and R 4.1.3.

sec.title: Role of funders
sec.p: The funders of the study had no role in the design and conduct of the study; in the data collection, management, analysis, and interpretation of the data; or in the writing, review, or approval of this manuscript.

sec.title: Study population
sec.p:
The nested case–control analysis included 1234 participants (617 hip fracture cases and 617 matched controls), with a predominantly white population (95.3%) and a mean age of 67 (SD = 8) years at blood collection (Table 1). The mean BMI was 25.4 ± 4.2 kg/m2. Of the total participants, 592 (48.0%) were male, 642 (52.0%) were female, and 191 (15.5%) reported a history of osteoporosis. While most covariates were balanced between cases and controls, differences were observed in alcohol intake (7 vs. 9 g/day), plasma vitamin D levels (26.8 vs. 28.1 ng/mL), and plasma sclerostin levels (47.7 vs. 51.5 pmol/L). sec.title: Metabolites and risk of hip fracture in the nested case‒control analysis
sec.p:
Fig. 1 shows the significant individual metabolites associated with hip fracture risk (P < 0.05). Among 653 plasma metabolites analysed (Supplementary Data S1), six phospholipid metabolism metabolites were associated with hip fracture risk (P < 0.05) across NHS and HPFS, with five showing an inverse association (1-palmitoyl-2-eicosapentaenoyl-glycerophosphocholine (GPC) (multivariable adjusted OR 0.82, 95% CI 0.73–0.93), 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC (OR 0.76, 95% CI 0.67–0.87), 1-pentadecanoyl-2-docosahexaenoyl-GPC (OR 0.84, 95% CI 0.74–0.95), 1-linoleoyl-2-docosahexaenoyl-GPC (OR 0.79, 95% CI 0.69–0.91), and 1-stearoyl-2-docosapentaenoyl-glycerophosphatidylethanolamine (GPE) (OR 0.83, 95% CI 0.74–0.95)) and one showing a positive association (1-oleyl-GPC) (OR 1.25, 95% CI 1.09–1.43) (Table 3). The direction and magnitude of these associations were consistent in both NHS and HPFS participants. After adjusting for multiple comparisons, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC remained statistically significant in the combined NHS and HPFS analysis (OR per SD increase: 0.76 [95% CI: 0.67–0.87]; FDR = 0.02) as shown in Fig. 1. The results remained largely consistent when height and weight were adjusted for separately instead of BMI (Table S4). Additionally, we found that 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC was inversely associated with history of falls among the NHS participants (Table S5).Fig. 1

sec.title: Metabolite classes and risk of hip fracture in the nested case‒control analysis
sec.p:
Ten metabolite classes were significantly associated with hip fracture risk in the combined NHS and HPFS analysis (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Data S2). Phosphatidylcholine (NES −2.2, FDR 0.01), phosphatidylethanolamine (NES −1.9, FDR 0.05), and fatty acid metabolism (acyl choline) (NES −1.9, FDR 0.03) classes were inversely associated with hip fracture risk, whereas exogenous chemical (NES 1.9, FDR 0.02), fatty acid (dicarboxylate) (NES 1.8, FDR 0.06), pregnenolone steroids (NES 1.6, FDR 0.07), acetylated peptides (NES 1.6, FDR 0.12), benzoate metabolism (NES 1.6, FDR 0.16), and food component (plant) (NES 1.7, FDR 0.05) classes were nominally and positively associated with risk. Although they did not reach statistical significance in NHS or HPFS, association directions were similar in NHS and HPFS. Phosphatidylcholine was consistently protective against hip fracture in both NHS and HPFS, with FDR values < 0.05 for enrichment scores. The associations between metabolite classes and hip fracture were consistent when stratified by the median time between blood collection and case diagnosis (Figure S4), i.e., cases occurring within or beyond 10 years since blood collection. Due to some metabolites not being measured in both NHS and HPFS, the associations for some metabolite classes were assessed in only one of the two cohorts.Fig. 2
Metabolite classes associated with hip fracture in the nested case‒control analysis of 1234 participants. A total of 10 metabolite classes were identified (FDR < 0.2) in the total population (HPFS + NHS), HPFS or NHS via metabolite set enrichment analysis (MSEA). Blank grids represent metabolite classes that were not assessed because less than 3 of the corresponding metabolites were measured in the population. The exogenous chemical class included exogenous miscellaneous chemicals such as drugs, environmental toxins, and dietary additives. The conditional logistic regression models were adjusted for age, BMI, alcohol intake, history of osteoporosis, plasma vitamin D level, plasma sclerostin level, and matching factors. Abbreviations: HPFS, Health Professionals Follow-Up Study; NHS, Nurses' Health Study; MSEA, metabolite set enrichment analysis; FDR, false discovery rate. ∗FDR < 0.2; ∗∗FDR < 0.05.

Four metabolites from the exogenous chemical class and five from the fatty acid (dicarboxylate) class were positively associated with hip fracture risk (Fig. 3A). Conversely, three metabolites from the fatty acid metabolism (acyl choline) class were inversely associated with hip fracture risk (Fig. 3B). The direction and magnitude of these associations between individual metabolites and hip fracture were consistent when stratified by the median time between blood collection and case diagnosis (Figure S5), i.e., cases occurring within or beyond 10 years since blood collection.Fig. 3
Metabolites of identified metabolite classes associated with hip fracture in the nested case‒control analysis of 1234 participants. A. Metabolites of metabolite classes that were positively associated with hip fracture. B. Metabolites of metabolite classes that were inversely associated with hip fracture. Metabolites significantly associated with hip fracture in the total population (HPFS + NHS), HPFS or NHS are presented in the plot. Blank grids represent the metabolites that were not measured in the population. The conditional logistic regression models were adjusted for age, BMI, alcohol intake, history of osteoporosis, plasma vitamin D level, and plasma sclerostin level. Abbreviations: HPFS, Health Professionals Follow-Up Study; NHS, Nurses' Health Study; OR, odds ratio. ∗P < 0.05; ∗∗FDR < 0.05.

Correlation analysis (Figure S6) showed minimal associations between phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine metabolites and clinical/dietary intake variables, including beta-C-terminal telopeptide, osteocalcin, sclerostin, parathyroid hormone, plasma calcium, plasma vitamin D, and dietary intake (Spearman r values: −0.2 to 0.2).

sec.title: Cohort analysis: replication
sec.p: During a median follow-up of 25.5 [IQR 20.3–26.3] years in the cohort study, 475 participants reported an incident hip fracture and 3517 were censored at death. Based on our findings from the case–control study, we tested the associations of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC and ten metabolite classes with incident hip fracture in the cohort study. Among these, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC and the metabolite classes phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine were also measured in the cohort study.

1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC (PC 38:3) was consistently inversely associated with hip fracture in the replication study driven by the HPFS participants (HR per SD increase: 0.65 [95% CI: 0.46–0.90], Fig. 4). Among the phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine classes, 3 phosphatidylcholine metabolites and 2 phosphatidylethanolamine metabolites were consistently inversely associated with hip fracture in the replication study, a greater number of significant metabolites were identified among HPFS participants (Fig. 4, Supplementary Data S3). These associations between metabolites and incident hip fracture were consistent when analysing cases occurring within or beyond 10 years since blood collection (Figure S7, Supplementary Data S4), when repeating the analysis restricted to the control groups of the 14 sub-studies in the cohort replication (Figure S8), or taking account of the competing risk of death (Table S6).Fig. 4
Association of individual metabolites of the phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine classes with the risk of hip fracture in the cohort replication analysis of 10,031 participants. Abbreviations: HPFS, Health Professionals Follow-Up Study; NHS, Nurses' Health Study; PC, phosphatidylcholine; PE, phosphatidylethanolamine; HR, hazard ratio. Blank grids represent the metabolites that were not measured in the population. The Cox proportional hazards models were adjusted for fasting status, season of blood collection, case control status, sub-study outcome, age, BMI, alcohol intake, postmenopausal status and hormone use (NHS only), and history of osteoporosis. C38:3 PC represents 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-γ-linolenoyl-GPC, the metabolite measured in the case–control analysis. ∗P < 0.05; ∗∗P < 0.01; ∗∗∗FDR < 0.05

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Our study investigated the relationship between plasma metabolomic profiles and hip fracture risk in females and males. We identified an inverse association between several metabolites in the phosphatidylcholine (PC) and phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) classes and the risk of hip fracture in the nested case–control analysis and in the replication cohort analysis. Additionally, 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, a specific phosphatidylcholine metabolite, was consistently associated with reduced fracture risk in the nested case–control study and was replicated in the cohort replication analysis. These findings support the hypothesis that dysregulated phospholipid metabolism contributes to fracture susceptibility.

Our study specifically focuses on prospective associations between plasma metabolites and hip fracture. A prior systematic review identified 16 studies linking metabolomic alterations to BMD and osteoporosis, many of which implicated amino acids (e.g., valine, leucine, glycine) in bone metabolism.15 These studies collectively assessed ∼400 unique metabolites in blood that were shown to be cross-sectionally associated with BMD. However, only one study examined metabolite associations with osteoporotic fractures, and it was limited by a small sample size and a lack of specificity for hip fracture.16 Previous studies also indicate that hip fracture risk is associated with a relatively limited set of metabolites, primarily amino acids,32 tryptophan-related metabolites,33 non-esterified fatty acids,34 and lipoproteins.35 By focussing on hip fracture, a major and most severe clinical outcome associated with osteoporosis, our study advances the field by identifying phospholipid metabolism as a key pathway. A prior systematic review36 also highlighted certain pathways, such as amino acids and fatty acid metabolism, that are potentially involved in the development of osteoporosis, which are supported by the our results. Furthermore, our replication in a cohort analysis strengthens the evidence for phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine metabolites as potential biomarkers of hip fracture risk.

The metabolites identified in our study differ in part from those previously reported in studies focused on BMD, such as the Framingham Osteoporosis Study and Hong Kong Osteoporosis Study.16 This divergence likely reflects the broader biological pathways underlying hip fracture risk, which extend beyond bone density to include factors such as falls, injury, muscle function, and cognition.37, 38, 39 In the NHS participants, we consistently found that 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC was inversely associated with fall history (Table S5). Although BMD remains a key determinant of fracture risk, it does not fully capture individual susceptibility, and certain metabolites may indicate fracture risk through BMD-independent mechanisms. The partial overlap we observed, including phosphatidylcholine, glycine, and sulphate metabolites associated with both BMD and hip fracture, supports shared but distinct metabolic pathways.16,40 Methodological differences, such as the use of the Metabolon platform analysing over 600 metabolites in this current study compared with ∼200 in earlier studies, may also contribute to variability in findings. Collectively, these results underscore the potential translational value of metabolomic profiling for uncovering biological mechanisms and identifying complementary biomarkers that could, with further validation, enhance risk stratification for hip fracture.

Emerging evidence suggests that alterations in lipid metabolism may play a critical role in bone fragility.41,42 Phosphatidylcholine and phosphatidylethanolamine, the two most abundant phospholipids in mammalian cells, are synthesised via the Kennedy pathway and are integral to cell membrane integrity and signalling.43 Our findings align with prior studies showing that phosphatidylcholine levels are linked to BMD and osteoporosis based on cross-sectional designs. A lipidomic study revealed that the most significantly dysregulated class associated with low BMD was phosphatidylcholines, accounting for 25.2% of the dysregulated lipid metabolites.44 Zhang et al. reported that the levels of phosphatidylcholine metabolites were inversely associated with BMD.16 In another metabolomics study of 265 named metabolites, the authors reported that phosphatidylcholine was associated with increased odds of low BMD.45 A meta-analysis indicated that phosphatidylcholine levels are increased in patients with osteopenia and osteoporosis.46 Our prospective analysis of hip fractures suggests the inverse association between the phosphatidylcholine class and metabolites and the risk of hip fracture. Interestingly, the protective associations of PC metabolites may depend on their fatty acid composition. For example, PC-linoleic acid has been linked to BMD loss, whereas PC-arachidonic acid may protect against osteoporosis. Our identification of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC as a key metabolite linked to fracture risk suggests that specific phosphatidylcholine metabolites may influence bone health via distinct mechanisms.47

Lysophosphatidylcholine class has been implicated in bone metabolism but with conflicting results.46 Our findings support a significant impact of a lysophosphatidylcholine metabolite on bone health, i.e., LPC (O-18:1), which was associated with increased hip fracture risk. Mechanistically, LPC is a component of oxidised low-density lipoprotein (ox-LDL) and can stimulate adipogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells (BMSCs), reducing osteoblast activity, thus accelerating the occurrence of osteoporosis.48 The conversion pathway of phosphatidylcholine to lysophosphatidylcholine by phospholipase A2 (PLA2) was shown to be overactivated in osteoarthritis.49 Prior genetic studies also supported the associations between LDL cholesterol, lipid-lowering medications, and BMD.50,51 Mechanistic studies also supported our findings showing that choline kinase β mutant mice, which lack a kinase involved in the biosynthesis of phosphatidylcholine, exhibit a systemic low-bone mass phenotype caused by increased bone resorption.52 A study using a Mendelian randomisation framework and mechanistic experiments consistently confirmed the causal relationship between phosphatidylcholine and BMSC proliferation and osteogenesis, thus reducing the risk of osteoporosis.53 Phospholipid metabolism is also closely involved in the treatment of osteogenesis by reducing adipogenic differentiation and promoting the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs via Wnt pathway activation and PPARγ pathway inhibition in ovariectomised rats.54 Notably, phosphatidylcholine metabolites have been linked to lower risks of cardiometabolic diseases and cognition decline, which are closely related with hip fracture.55, 56, 57, 58

In terms of individual metabolites, the identification of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomolinolenoyl-GPC (18:0/20:3n3 or 6), discovered in our nested case‒control analysis and replicated in the cohort analysis as a key metabolite, might be a biomarker and potential intervention target to prevent hip fracture. A prior study revealed associations between 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC, physical activity, and body mass index, which may play a role in mediating the health effects of physical activity and muscle strength on hip fractures.59 Using multimodal data, Shomorony et al. reported that 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC is also involved in metabolic health, which is closely correlated with bone and muscle health.60,61 More data on this specific metabolite and health profiles are needed.

Phosphatidylethanolamine, which comprises ∼25% of total phospholipids in eukaryotic cells, also exhibited a strong inverse association with hip fracture risk. Specifically, 1-stearoyl-2-docosapentaenoyl-GPE and 1-enyl-stearoyl-2-docosahexaenoyl-GPE were associated with lower risk of hip fracture, though some PE metabolites have been linked to metabolic syndrome and diabetes.62,63 Phosphatidylethanolamine metabolites have also been indicated as potential biomarkers for Alzheimer's disease, which may in turn impact the risk of fractures.64

Our study also identified fatty acid metabolism (acyl choline) as inversely associated with hip fracture, including stearoylcholine, dihomolenoyl choline, and arachidonoylcholine. These findings align with previous research demonstrating that trans fatty acids, short-chain saturated lipids (e.g., palmitic acid, stearic acid), and polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFA, e.g., linoleic acid, eicosapentaenoic acid, docosahexaenoic acid) play critical roles in bone metabolism.6,34,47,65,66 However, prior cohort studies have yielded mixed results regarding omega-3 PUFA intake and fracture prevention.67,68 Conversely, fatty acid dicarboxylates (e.g., hexadecanedioate, octadecanedioate, dodecanedioate) were positively associated with hip fracture risk. These metabolites are produced via ω-oxidation of fatty acids and have been linked to BMD regulation in Mendelian randomisation studies.69 Further research is needed to elucidate their precise role in bone fragility.

The strength of our study lies in its use of a well-designed nested case‒control study to investigate the prospective associations between metabolite profiles and the risk of hip fracture. We replicated our findings using two large, well-characterised cohorts with long-term follow-up, coupled with the integration of high-throughput metabolomics.

Even though this is a prospective analysis, we cannot fully exclude the role of residual or unmeasured confounding. Residual confounding due to measurement error in self-reported covariates, such as alcohol intake and other lifestyle factors, cannot be excluded. More mechanistic studies are needed to further shed light on mechanisms underlying our findings. While our results were partially replicated in the cohort analysis, future studies should aim to replicate these findings in other populations and investigate whether incorporating metabolite measures, alongside established risk factors such as BMD and FRAX scores, can improve fracture risk assessment. As these clinical prediction scores and BMD data were not routinely available in the NHS and HPFS cohorts, our study primarily focused on identifying metabolites associated with hip fracture risk. Future studies are needed to elucidate the roles of BMD in the association between identified metabolites and risk of hip fracture. Moreover, further data are required to evaluate and compare the hip fracture prediction capacity of plasma metabolomics with other omics technologies, including polygenic risk scores and proteomics.70 Additionally, the availability of plasma metabolite measurements at a single timepoint limits our ability to assess how changes in specific metabolite classes and individual metabolite concentrations over time may affect the outcome of hip fracture. Our analysis is also limited to hip fracture, which is particularly associated with significant morbidity and mortality,71 so our findings should be replicated at other bone and fracture sites. Further studies are needed to explore the underlying mechanisms and evaluate the effect of phosphatidylcholine as an intervention to prevent hip fractures.

In conclusion, this study provides the prospective evidence that altered phospholipid metabolism, particularly phosphatidylcholine, is associated with reduced hip fracture risk in both females and males. Our identification of 1-stearoyl-2-dihomo-linolenoyl-GPC as a key protective metabolite implicates specific metabolic pathways in hip fracture risk. These findings highlight the potential of plasma metabolomics in identifying novel risk factors for hip fractures and may inform the development of metabolite-based interventions for fracture prevention in ageing populations.

sec.title: Data sharing statement
sec.p: Owing to participant confidentiality and privacy concerns, data cannot be shared publicly and requests to access NHS/NHSII/HPFS data must be submitted in writing. According to standard controlled access procedures, applications to use NHS/NHSII/HPFS resources will be reviewed by the External Collaborations Committee to verify that the proposed use maintains the protection of the privacy of participants and the confidentiality of the data. Investigators wishing to use NHS/NHSII/HPFS data are asked to submit a brief description of the proposed project. Further information including the procedures to obtain and access data from the Nurses’ Health Studies and Health Professionals Follow-up Study is described at https://www.nurseshealthstudy.org/researchers and https://hsph.harvard.edu/research/health-professionals.
